did_you_know.text: The opening 'These are the journeys' turns the chapter into an itinerary — like a travel map of a people in the desert.
It says Moses wrote their departures 'by the LORD' — indicating the list was meant as an official, organized record.
'Rameses' is a place in Egypt, and the departure 'on the day after Passover' ties the timing to the Israelites' religious calendar.
The verse notes that the Egyptians buried the dead — burial rites were important to them — and the text adds that their gods were judged as well.
Here 'Sukkot' is a place-name; later the festival of Sukkot recalls the booths in which Israelites lived in the wilderness.
The phrase 'a three days' journey' recurs in the Bible; a three-day march often marks a significant transition in desert travel.
Elim's 'twelve springs and seventy palms' — the numbers 12 and 70 are often seen as symbolic (e.g., 12 for the tribes, 70 a significant number in ancient tradition).
The term 'Yam Suf' is sometimes translated 'Red Sea' and sometimes 'Sea of Reeds' — it does not necessarily mean the modern Red Sea on maps.
At Rephidim it says there was no water — at this same site a later story recounts the miracle of water from the rock (Exodus 17).
The 'wilderness of Sinai' is more than a stop — it becomes the central setting for the giving of the law and people’s legislation.
The name 'Kivrot‑HaTaavah' literally means 'graves of craving' — the name preserves the memory of complaints and desires associated with the journey.
'Hazeroth' appears elsewhere as the place where Miriam and Aaron complain about Moses (see Numbers 12).
Kadesh (Kadesh‑Barnea) is a major campsite in the journeys — from here the spies were later sent into Canaan.
Aaron's death on the mountain marks not only his end but also the transfer of the priesthood to his son Eleazar (reported elsewhere in the narrative tradition).
This verse gives a precise date — 'in the fortieth year' on the first day of the fifth month — which helps construct the Exodus and journey chronology.
Arad, the Canaanite king in the Negev, may correspond to the archaeological site Tel Arad where Canaanite remains have been found.
The encampment on the plains of Moab by the Jordan is the setting where Moses delivers his final speeches that form the book of Deuteronomy.
The command to cross the Jordan signals a turning point: the desert wanderings are ending and the people are about to enter and possess a new land.
The warning not to leave the inhabitants is meant to prevent their religious and cultural influence on Israel — a concern repeated elsewhere in the biblical literature.
